Uma cena que você já viveu (ou vai viver: A scene you have lived (or will). You already know how to conjugate verbs, use the past, the future and the accusative case. Now imagine another scene. You are in Russia. You want to say you are in your room. You think: "room in Russian is ко́мната. I'll say я в ко́мната." The person gives you a strange look and corrects you: — Я в ко́мнате. You look again. It is the same word, ко́мната. But now it ends in -е, not -а. You think: "Why? I already changed this word for the accusative (ко́мнату). Has it changed again? How many forms does this word have?" This happens to every Russian learner, and it happens because you have just met the prepositional case. It sounds like one more complicated case. It is not. Five minutes of careful reading and you will understand the little secret that solves everything. What is the prepositional case, and why is it called that? First, a question: why is this case called prepositional? Memorise this: the prepositional case is the only case in Russian that NEVER appears alone. It always comes after a preposition. That is where the name comes from: it is the case "of the preposition". It does not exist without one. Never, in any sentence, in any context. The nominative can appear alone (это дом), the accusative can appear alone (я вижу дом), but the prepositional always has a preposition before it. Always. And what is it for? Here is the answer: the prepositional case is used to say WHERE things are. It is the case of place. When you want to say "I am in the room", "I live in Russia", "the book is on the table", "I work at the factory", in all of these sentences the noun goes into the prepositional case. It is the "where" case. As simple as that. (It is also used with the preposition «о» to say what you are talking or thinking "about".) English puts all the meaning in the little words "in", "on", "at", and the noun never changes. Russian changes both the little word and the ending of the noun.
O segredinho: lugares abertos e lugares: The little secret: open places and closed places

The little secret: open places and closed places. Now comes the most charming part. Pay attention, because here is the key to everything. Russian has two main prepositions for "where": В and НА. Both can mean "in", "on" or "at". But Russian chooses between them with a very simple logic. В → for CLOSED places: places you can go inside, places with walls, doors, an interior. НА → for OPEN, WIDE places: places where you are on, on top of, on the surface. The magic test: ask yourself, can you go inside? YES → В (shop, room, cinema, theatre, house, school, factory, restaurant, museum...). NO, it is a wide, open place → НА (square, street, park, station, market, mountain, river...). Look at how it works. Комната (room): you can go inside → В. Магазин (shop): you can go inside → В. Площадь (square): wide, open → НА. Улица (street): open → НА. Работа (work): not a physical place but an activity → НА. Урок (lesson): not a place but an event → НА. Концерт (concert): not a place but an event → НА. The general rule: can you go inside? If yes, В. If it is wide, open, or an event or activity, НА. English does something similar, only less neatly: you are "in" the room but "on" the street, "at" the station, "at" a concert, "at" work. (A few words, like почта, break the logic. Learn them as exceptions.)

A ponte com o português: В = no/na: The bridge with English: В = in, НА = on / at
A ponte com o português: В = no/na. Aqui: The bridge with English: В = in, НА = on / at. Here is the nicest thing: you already do this in English without noticing. You say: I am in the room. I am in the shop. I am in the cinema. I am on the square. I am on the street. I am at the station. English picks "in", "on" or "at" depending on the place, and sometimes it is hard to explain why (on the bus, in the car, at work). Russian does the same with just two words. The preposition В works like our "in". The preposition НА works like our "on / at", with a nuance of "on top of, on the surface". Compare. Notice that the preposition is a separate word, never merged into the noun. But the idea is the same as in English. You only have to choose between В (closed) and НА (open / event). And do not forget the second half: the noun changes its ending (комната → комнате).
I'm on top of the room.
I'm on top of the shop.
I'm on top of the cinema.
As 4 principais preposições do prepositi: The 4 main prepositions of the prepositional case

The 4 main prepositions of the prepositional case. The prepositional case is governed by four main prepositions. Let's meet each one. • 1. В (in, inside). Use: closed places you can go inside. Question: Где? (Where?) Examples follow. Spelling variant: ВО. Before words that begin with в or ф followed by another consonant, ВО is used instead of В. Why? Euphony. Russian does not like certain consonant clusters: «в Владивостоке» would sound bad, so an -о- is inserted to separate them. • 2. НА (on, at). Use: open, wide places, or events and activities. Question: Где? (Where?) Examples follow. Notice that на also appears with places that "make no sense" (почта, работа, урок, концерт). The logic is not only "open vs. closed": it also includes events, activities and surfaces. And there are historical exceptions, which we will see later. • 3. О (about, concerning). Use: to talk about something. Question: О ком? О чём? (About whom? About what?) Examples follow. Spelling variants: ОБ and ОБО. О goes before a consonant: о кни́ге, о рабо́те, о теа́тре. ОБ goes before a vowel: об Ива́не, об А́нне, об э́том, об о́сени. ОБО goes before мне, всём, всех and a few other words that start with a hard consonant cluster: обо мне, обо всём, обо льде. Why? Euphony again. «О Иване» would sound bad, and «о мне» too. So Russian inserts об or обо to keep the vowels and consonants apart. (You do this in English with "a" / "an": a book, an apple.) • 4. ПРИ (at, in the presence of, in the time of). Use: rare in daily life, but it appears in formal and historical contexts and in contexts of closeness. ПРИ has three meanings: • 1. Attached to, next to: при университе́те (attached to the university). • 2. In the presence of: при де́тях (in front of the children). • 3. In the time of: при царе́ (in the time of the tsar).
In the time of Tsar Nicholas...
In the time of Peter I...
Next to the university there is a library.
Don't say that in front of the children.
в e на: escolher pela imagem do lugar: в and на: choosing by the picture of the place
Os dois significam «em», mas o russo esc: Both mean «in / at / on», but Russian chooses by picture. «В» = inside a closed or bounded space: в доме, в комнате, в сумке, and also countries and cities (в России, в Москве). «На» = on a surface (на столе, на полу, на стене), in a place seen as open space (на улице, на площади, на море) or at an event or activity (на работе, на уроке, на концерте). The word after в/на goes into the prepositional case (-е, -и): в доме, на столе. Some short masculine nouns have a prepositional in -у when they answer «где?»: в шкафу, в саду, в лесу, на полу, на мосту.
em português usamos «em / na / no» para: English also uses «in / on / at», but not in the same places: Russian says «на работе» (literally «on work») and «на уроке» (literally «on the lesson»). The choice between в and на depends on the picture of the place: inside, on top, open space or event.
On top of a surface: на.

A regra da tesourinha do prepositivo: The scissors rule of the prepositional
A regra da tesourinha do prepositivo. Ag: The scissors rule of the prepositional. Now the mechanics. How does the noun change when it goes into the prepositional? The scissors work as always: • 1. Find the nominative form (the dictionary word). • 2. Apply the prepositional ending, which depends on the gender and on the ending. • 3. Done. The noun is in the prepositional. Look at the endings in the table. Notice that the rule is almost always -Е. Only feminine nouns in -ь and nouns in -ия/-ие take -И (written -ИИ for those in -ия/-ие). And neuter nouns in -мя take -ЕНИ. Let's look at each case in detail.
O MASCULINO no prepositivo. O masculino: The MASCULINE in the prepositional. The masculine is the easiest: always -Е. It does not matter whether it ends in a consonant, in -й or in -ь. The ending is -Е. Masculine in a consonant: pay attention to the stress. стол → столе́ (the stress moves to the ending); дом → до́ме (the stress stays on the stem). There is no fixed rule. You need to listen and memorise. Masculine in -ь: notice that the -ь disappears and -е comes in. Always. Masculine in -й: notice that the -й disappears and -е comes in.
O FEMININO no prepositivo. O feminino é: The FEMININE in the prepositional. The feminine is a little more complex, because it depends on the ending. Feminine in -а: notice that the -а disappears and -е comes in. Feminine in -я: the -я disappears and -е comes in. Feminine in -ь → ending -И. Here is the exception: a feminine noun in -ь gets -И, not -е. The -ь disappears and -и comes in. Always. Feminine in -ия → ending -ИИ. Words in -ия get -ии (two "i"s). The -я disappears and -ии comes in. (A few feminine nouns in -ь also move the stress: любовь → о любви́.)
Neutro e tabela mestra do prepositivo: The neuter and the master table of the prepositional
O NEUTRO no prepositivo. O neutro é o ma: The NEUTER in the prepositional. The neuter is the simplest. Two rules. Neuter in -о: notice that the -о becomes -е. Always. Neuter in -е: words in -е usually stay the same. But words in -ие (with an "i" before the "e") get -ии: упражне́ние → упражне́нии, зна́ние → зна́нии, зда́ние → зда́нии. Why? The same logic as -ия → -ии. Neuter in -мя → ending -ЕНИ. Neuter words ending in -мя get -ени. There are about 10 of them, and you already know them from lesson 11. They are neuter and end in -мя. In the prepositional they become -мени. The master table of the prepositional. Here is the table that solves everything.
A tabela mestra do prepositivo: The master table of the prepositional
Onde está? лежать, стоять, сидеть, висет: Where is it? лежать, стоять, сидеть, висеть
Em português dizemos «está» para tudo: «: In English we say «is» for everything: «the book is on the table». In Russian the verb chooses the position of the object: «лежать» (lying, horizontal), «стоять» (standing), «сидеть» (sitting), «висеть» (hanging). To sound natural, avoid «есть» and use the right verb: «Книга лежит на столе», «Лампа стоит на столе», «Кот сидит на диване», «Картина висит на стене». These verbs are 2nd conjugation: лежу, лежишь, лежит, лежим, лежите, лежат; сижу, сидишь...; стою, стоишь...; вишу, висишь...
o português usa «estar» para todas as po: English uses «is» (or «sits», «hangs») for position, but Russian always says whether the object is lying, standing, sitting or hanging.
Descreva uma sala em voz alta: «На столе: Describe a room out loud: «На столе лежит книга. На диване сидит кот. На стене висит картина.» Swap in other words.
The question "where?" versus "where to?". Here is one of the most important things in the whole lesson. Pay attention. Russian distinguishes between where (place) and where to (movement), and that distinction changes the case. ГДЕ? (Where?) → prepositional. You are already at the place. КУДА? (Where to?) → accusative. You are going to the place. English does the same with its little words: "in the room" (place) versus "into the room" or "to the room" (movement). Russian does it by changing the case after the same preposition. The rule: В + prepositional = "in / at" (where). В + accusative = "to / into" (where to). НА + prepositional = "on / at" (where). НА + accusative = "to / onto" (where to). It is the same preposition, but the case changes with the meaning. If it is a place, prepositional. If it is movement, accusative. Practical examples follow. That is all. The same preposition В or НА changes the case of the noun according to the meaning. Place → prepositional. Movement → accusative.
He is going to the shop (movement).
We are going to the square (movement).
He is going to the theatre.
As exceções: os irregulares em -У/-Ю: The exceptions: the irregular nouns in -У/-Ю
As exceções: os irregulares em -У/-Ю. Aq: The exceptions: the irregular nouns in -У/-Ю. Here is a point that is rarely explained well. A few masculine nouns take -У (or -Ю) in the prepositional, instead of -Е. But careful: only when the preposition is В or НА. With О, they go back to -Е. Look at the list of the most common irregular ones: the ending is -У (always stressed), and it only works with В and НА. Compare. The rule: when В/НА mean a place, these nouns use -У. When О means "about", they use the normal -Е. They have a split personality. Example sentences follow.
Tabelas de apoio e erros comuns no prepo: Support tables and common mistakes in the prepositional
B Tabelas de apoio: Adjetivos, Possessiv: Support tables: adjectives, possessives, pronouns and transport in the prepositional. Pronouns with О (about): обо мне · о тебе́ · о нём · о ней · о нас · о вас · о них. Means of transport (НА + prepositional): е́хать на авто́бусе, на метро́, на маши́не, на по́езде, на такси́; лете́ть на самолёте. The mistakes English speakers WILL make in the prepositional. Mistake 1: using the accusative instead of the prepositional. ❌ Wrong: Я в ко́мнату (meaning "I am in the room"). ✅ Right: Я в ко́мнате. You learned the accusative first (lesson 14) and tend to use the accusative ending for everything. But "I am in the room" is place, not movement, so it is prepositional. Mistake 2: using no preposition at all. ❌ Wrong: Я ко́мнате. ✅ Right: Я в ко́мнате. The prepositional never appears alone. It always comes with a preposition (В, НА, О, ПРИ). Without a preposition there is no prepositional. Mistake 3: using В instead of НА (and vice versa). ❌ Wrong: Я в пло́щади. ✅ Right: Я на пло́щади. A square is an open place, so it takes НА. The rule of open versus closed places solves 90% of this. Mistake 4: forgetting that a feminine in -ь takes -И, not -Е. ❌ Wrong: Я в но́че. ✅ Right: Я в но́чи. Mistake 5: forgetting that -ия takes -ии. ❌ Wrong: Я в Росси́е. ✅ Right: Я в Росси́и. Mistake 6: using О when the next word begins with a vowel. ❌ Wrong: Я говорю́ о Ива́не. ✅ Right: Я говорю́ об Ива́не. Before a vowel, О becomes ОБ, for euphony (like English "a" versus "an"). Mistake 7: using ОБ instead of ОБО. ❌ Wrong: Я говорю́ об мне. ✅ Right: Я говорю́ обо мне. Before мне, всём, всех and a few other words that begin with a consonant cluster, use ОБО. Mistake 8: forgetting that -мя takes -ени. ❌ Wrong: Я в вре́мя. ✅ Right: Я во вре́мени. Words in -мя get -ени in the prepositional, and В becomes ВО before this word. Mistake 9: confusing "where" and "where to". ❌ Wrong: Я иду́ в ко́мнате (meaning "I am going into the room"). ✅ Right: Я иду́ в ко́мнату. "I am going into the room" is movement → accusative. "I am in the room" is place → prepositional. Mistake 10: using -у/-ю with О. ❌ Wrong: Я говорю́ о лесу́. ✅ Right: Я говорю́ о ле́се. The irregular nouns in -у/-ю only work with В/НА. With О they go back to -е.
